lessonTitle: Digestion and Absorption of Carbohydrate, Protein and Fat

blocks.text: A healthy adult swallows several hundred grams of starch, protein and fat each day and loses only a few grams of it in the stool. A loaf of bread, a steak and a slab of butter must each be broken into units small enough to cross a single layer of cells. Digestion needs the right enzyme in the right place, and absorption needs the right transporter in the right membrane.

blocks.markdown: **The general plan.** Food macronutrients are polymers or large lipids that cannot cross the intestinal epithelium. Digestion has two stages. **Luminal (cavity) digestion** uses enzymes secreted by the salivary glands, stomach and pancreas. **Membrane (brush border) digestion** uses enzymes anchored to the microvilli of enterocytes. Products are absorbed across the **apical** membrane, processed in the cell, and leave across the **basolateral** membrane into the portal blood or lymph. The huge surface area of the small intestine, produced by folds, villi and microvilli (about 200 m2 in total), makes this possible, and most absorption is finished by the mid-jejunum.

blocks.title: Digestion versus absorption
blocks.text: Digestion is the chemical breakdown of food to absorbable units: monosaccharides, amino acids with small peptides, and monoglycerides with free fatty acids. Absorption is the transport of those units, with electrolytes, water and vitamins, across the epithelium into blood or lymph.

blocks.markdown:
**Carbohydrate.** Starch is digested by **salivary** and **pancreatic alpha-amylase** to maltose, maltotriose and alpha-limit dextrins; the pancreatic enzyme does the bulk of the work. Brush border enzymes finish the job: **maltase**, **sucrase-isomaltase** (the latter also splits alpha-limit dextrins), **lactase** (lactose to glucose and galactose) and trehalase. Only monosaccharides are absorbed. **Glucose and galactose** enter via **SGLT1**, a sodium-coupled symporter (2 Na+ per glucose) driven by the low intracellular sodium maintained by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase; **fructose** enters by facilitated diffusion through **GLUT5**. All three leave across the basolateral membrane through **GLUT2**.

**Protein.** Pepsin starts digestion in the stomach. In the duodenum pancreatic endopeptidases (**trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase**) and exopeptidases (**carboxypeptidases**) produce small peptides and amino acids; brush border aminopeptidases and dipeptidases finish. Free amino acids are absorbed by Na+-coupled transporters, and di- and tripeptides by the H+-coupled transporter **PEPT1**; cytosolic peptidases then reduce the peptides to amino acids, which exit basolaterally to the portal vein.

**Fat.** Dietary fat is mostly triglyceride and is insoluble in water, so it needs three steps.

1. **Emulsification:** gastric churning and bile salts break fat into small droplets, increasing surface area.
2. **Lipolysis:** pancreatic **lipase**, anchored to the droplet by **colipase**, removes the fatty acids at positions 1 and 3, leaving one **2-monoglyceride** and two **free fatty acids** per triglyceride.
3. **Micellar solubilisation:** conjugated **bile salts**, which are amphipathic, aggregate above their critical micellar concentration into **mixed micelles** that dissolve monoglycerides, fatty acids, cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K). Micelles carry these across the unstirred water layer to the brush border; the lipids diffuse or are transported into the cell, but the bile salts themselves are left behind and reabsorbed later in the ileum.

Inside the enterocyte, lipids are re-esterified to triglyceride in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and packaged with apolipoprotein B-48 into **chylomicrons**, which leave by exocytosis into the **lacteals** (lymph) and reach the blood through the thoracic duct. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are more water-soluble and go directly to the portal blood.

Micellar delivery; diffusion/transport of fatty acids and monoglycerides

blocks.title: Fat absorption coefficient
blocks.prompt: A patient eating 90 g of fat per day excretes 18 g of fat in the faeces per day. Calculate the percentage of dietary fat absorbed and decide whether this is steatorrhoea (faecal fat above about 7 g/day on a normal fat intake; thresholds vary).

steps.text: Compare with normal: healthy adults absorb about 95% or more, and faecal fat of 18 g/day exceeds 7 g/day, so this is fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea).

blocks.answer: 80% absorbed; this is steatorrhoea, indicating fat malabsorption.

blocks.title: Absorbing a sucrose meal
blocks.prompt: Sucrose is eaten. Trace its digestion and absorption, naming the enzyme and the transporters.

steps.text: Sucrose is not hydrolysed in the lumen to a significant extent; brush border sucrase-isomaltase splits it into one glucose and one fructose.
Glucose is taken up at the apical membrane by SGLT1 with 2 Na+ (energy from the Na+ gradient set by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase), while fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5.
Both sugars leave through GLUT2 on the basolateral membrane and enter the portal blood.

blocks.answer: Brush border sucrase-isomaltase gives glucose and fructose; SGLT1 takes up glucose, GLUT5 takes up fructose, GLUT2 exports both to the portal vein.

items: Carbohydrate: amylase then brush border disaccharidases; only monosaccharides are absorbed (SGLT1, GLUT5, GLUT2).
Protein: pepsin, pancreatic proteases, then brush border peptidases; amino acids and di/tripeptides (PEPT1) are absorbed.
Fat: bile salt emulsification, pancreatic lipase and colipase, micelles, re-esterification, chylomicrons to lymph.
Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) follow fat and need micelles.
Lactase deficiency and coeliac disease cause malabsorption by different mechanisms: missing enzyme versus reduced surface.

blocks.title: Lactase deficiency versus coeliac disease
blocks.text: In lactase deficiency, lactose is not hydrolysed, so it stays in the lumen, acts as an osmotic load and is fermented by colonic bacteria to gas and organic acids, giving bloating and watery diarrhoea only after lactose. In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten damages the small-intestinal mucosa (villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia), reducing the absorptive surface and brush border enzymes for all nutrients, with malabsorption of fat, iron and folate. Reference tests include a hydrogen breath test for lactose and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies with biopsy for coeliac disease.

blocks.title: Two different routes into the body
blocks.text: Do not say all absorbed nutrients go to the liver first. Glucose, amino acids and short-chain fatty acids enter portal blood, but long-chain fat leaves the enterocyte in chylomicrons that enter lymph and bypass the portal vein initially.

points: Starch is cleaved by amylase and brush border enzymes to glucose, galactose and fructose, absorbed via SGLT1 (with 2 Na+) or GLUT5 and exported by GLUT2.
Proteins are digested by pepsin, pancreatic proteases and brush border peptidases; amino acids and di/tripeptides (PEPT1) are absorbed and enter portal blood.
Fat digestion needs bile salt emulsification, pancreatic lipase with colipase and mixed micelles; triglycerides are rebuilt in enterocytes and exported as chylomicrons into lymph.
Lactase deficiency causes osmotic and fermentative diarrhoea after lactose, whereas coeliac disease reduces the absorptive surface by villous atrophy.

questions.stem: Which transporter carries glucose across the apical membrane of the enterocyte, coupled to sodium?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: SGLT1 is a Na+-glucose symporter on the apical membrane.
distractorRationale.b: GLUT2 is the basolateral exit route.
distractorRationale.c: GLUT5 transports fructose by facilitated diffusion.
distractorRationale.d: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and fat.

questions.explanation: SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient maintained by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase to drive glucose and galactose into the enterocyte. GLUT2 then allows the sugars to leave across the basolateral membrane.

questions.stem: A patient with obstruction of the common bile duct has bulky pale stools that float. Which statement best explains the fat malabsorption?

options.text: Without bile salts, mixed micelles cannot form, so monoglycerides and fatty acids are poorly solubilised and delivered to the mucosa
Without bile salts, triglyceride is not hydrolysed to glycerol and fatty acids by amylase
Without bile salts, chylomicrons cannot enter the portal vein
Without bile salts, GLUT5 cannot transport fructose

questions.correctOptionText: Without bile salts, mixed micelles cannot form, so monoglycerides and fatty acids are poorly solubilised and delivered to the mucosa

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles that carry lipolysis products across the unstirred layer.
distractorRationale.b: Triglyceride is hydrolysed by pancreatic lipase, not amylase.
distractorRationale.c: Chylomicrons enter lymph, not the portal vein, and this is unrelated to bile obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: GLUT5 and fructose are unrelated to fat absorption.

questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fat and form mixed micelles above their critical micellar concentration. Without them, the products of lipolysis cannot be carried efficiently to the brush border, causing fat in the stool (steatorrhoea) and poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old develops bloating, flatulence and watery stools within hours of drinking milk. Stool pH is acidic and a hydrogen breath test is positive after a lactose load. Which mechanism best explains the diarrhoea?

options.text: Unhydrolysed lactose remains in the lumen as an osmotic load and is fermented by colonic bacteria
Destruction of intestinal villi by gluten
Excess SGLT1 activity causing glucose secretion

questions.correctOptionText: Unhydrolysed lactose remains in the lumen as an osmotic load and is fermented by colonic bacteria

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lactase deficiency leaves lactose unabsorbed, drawing water and generating gas and acids.
distractorRationale.b: Lactose is not digested by amylase; it needs brush border lactase.
distractorRationale.c: This describes coeliac disease, which would not be limited to milk.
distractorRationale.d: SGLT1 absorbs glucose and does not secrete it.

questions.explanation: Without brush border lactase, lactose cannot be split into absorbable glucose and galactose. It draws water into the lumen osmotically and is fermented in the colon, producing hydrogen (breath test) and acidic stool.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea, iron-deficiency anaemia and weight loss. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are positive and a duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Which statement best explains her malabsorption?

options.text: Loss of villi reduces absorptive surface area and brush border enzymes for many nutrients
A single missing brush border enzyme prevents absorption of one sugar only
Failure of the pancreas to secrete lipase
Increased reabsorption of bile salts in the colon

questions.correctOptionText: Loss of villi reduces absorptive surface area and brush border enzymes for many nutrients

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the mucosal lesion is generalised, so fat, iron, folate and other nutrients are affected.
distractorRationale.b: This describes a selective enzyme deficiency such as lactase deficiency.
distractorRationale.c: Pancreatic insufficiency is not the primary problem here.
distractorRationale.d: Bile salt reabsorption in the colon does not explain this picture.

questions.explanation: In coeliac disease, immune injury triggered by gluten flattens villi and shortens the surface available for absorption, and brush border enzyme activity falls. That produces generalised malabsorption, in contrast to the single-sugar effect of lactase deficiency.

questions.stem: Di- and tripeptides can be absorbed by the enterocyte through the H+-coupled transporter PEPT1.
questions.explanation: PEPT1 on the apical membrane takes up di- and tripeptides, and cytosolic peptidases then split them into amino acids. Free amino acids use separate Na+-coupled transporters.

questions.stem: A patient eats 80 g of fat per day and excretes 12 g of fat per day in the faeces. What percentage of dietary fat is absorbed?
questions.explanation: The amount absorbed is 80 - 12 = 68 g/day, and 68/80 x 100 = 85%. Healthy adults absorb roughly 95% or more, and faecal fat above about 7 g/day indicates steatorrhoea, so this fits fat malabsorption.

questions.stem: A person with lactase deficiency drinks a solution containing 25 g of lactose (molar mass 342 g/mol). Assume 70% of the lactose is not hydrolysed or absorbed and passes on into the colon. How many mmol of lactose reach the colon?
questions.explanation: The unabsorbed mass is 0.70 x 25 g = 17.5 g, and 17.5 g / 342 g/mol = 0.0512 mol = about 51 mmol. This osmotically active load draws water into the lumen and is fermented by bacteria, producing the diarrhoea and gas.

questions.stem: Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrate and protein, naming the enzymes involved and the transporters on the apical and basolateral membranes.
markingGuide: Starch digested by salivary and pancreatic alpha-amylase to maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins
Brush border maltase, sucrase-isomaltase and lactase produce monosaccharides
Glucose and galactose absorbed by SGLT1 (Na+ coupled, 2 Na+ per sugar); fructose by GLUT5; export via basolateral GLUT2
Protein digested by pepsin then pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidases, then brush border peptidases
Amino acids absorbed by Na+-coupled transporters and di/tripeptides by PEPT1; cytosolic peptidases; amino acids exit basolaterally to the portal vein
questions.explanation: Both macronutrients follow a pattern: polymer to oligomer in the lumen, oligomer to monomer at the brush border, then transporters at the apical and basolateral membranes. Sodium gradients created by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase drive many of the apical steps.

questions.stem: Explain why bile salts and micelles are needed for normal fat absorption, and predict two consequences of bile salt deficiency.
markingGuide: Bile salts emulsify fat droplets, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase (with colipase)
Lipase produces 2-monoglyceride and free fatty acids, which are poorly soluble in water
Above the critical micellar concentration bile salts form mixed micelles that solubilise monoglycerides, fatty acids, cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins
Micelles carry lipids across the unstirred water layer to the brush border for uptake; bile salts are recycled to the ileum
Consequences: steatorrhoea (pale, bulky, floating stools) and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K (for example bleeding from low vitamin K)
questions.explanation: Fat is insoluble, so it needs both emulsification and a carrier to reach the epithelium. Without bile salts the products of lipolysis stay in oil droplets, and fat and fat-soluble vitamins are lost in stool.

questions.stem: Explain why absorbed glucose and long-chain dietary fat reach the circulation by different routes, and say where short-chain fatty acids go.
markingGuide: Glucose is water-soluble and leaves the enterocyte via GLUT2 into capillaries, then the portal vein to the liver
Long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides are re-esterified to triglyceride in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Triglyceride is packaged with apolipoprotein B-48, cholesterol and phospholipid into chylomicrons
Chylomicrons are too large for capillary pores, so they exit by exocytosis into lacteals and travel via lymph and the thoracic duct to the venous circulation
Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are more water-soluble and go directly into portal blood
questions.explanation: Route follows solubility and particle size. Small water-soluble molecules cross capillary walls, whereas large lipoprotein particles must enter the more permeable lymphatic lacteals.
